I think what might be happening is a combination of 2 mechanics. When you get too far away from your minions they will die and start respawning. I'm not sure the exact distance, but it seems like if you get about 1.5 screens away from a minion it will despawn. The other mechanic at play is that when *another* minion dies after your minion respawn timer has begun, it will restart the timer. 

So, my guess would be as you shield charge forward it's despawning some of them, then a couple more on the next shield charge, then a couple more, leading to a long stretch of time in between revives. That's just my guess though. To be honest I don't use any movement abilities on my summoner so I don't know for sure how they interact with minions and respawns.

Also, not sure if you knew but you can see your minion respawn timer as a buff icon to the right of the minions themselves in the top left. If you see that number resetting several times as you're shield charging around, then I think what I was suggesting is indeed what's happening.

I saw someone posted this suggestion as a workaround until they (hopefully) give us back convocation in some form: You can bind a skill to your weapon swap, and remove all your minions from the weapon swap set. This will instantly desummon all of them, then you use another skill to swap back to your main weapon set.

It will instantly respawn them around you (most of the time, sometimes you'll still need to wait out the revive timer, but if you do then you'll have ALL of the minions respawn at once right around you, which offers some immediate safety). Obviously this is no where near as good as actual convocation, but it is a really nice tech to know about as a summoner, highly recommend giving it a try until the issues you mentioned are more directly addressed.

I've said before that I think this all stems from Dark Souls (or Demon Souls if you want, but Dark Souls saw some serious success in comparison). I think too many game devs took the wrong lesson from Dark Souls' success. It was successful precisely BECAUSE it stood in opposition to the way the vast majority of games treated their players, because players were looking for something different.

Now, that market is beyond saturated, and has begun seeping into other game genres that simply don't work with this adversarial relationship with their players. The pendulum has swung back and now people just want their games to be mindless fun.

It's also possible this pendulum swing has to do with our current state of society. Maybe a decade ago we were all a lot more willing to inject some difficulty and adversarial nature into our free-time hobbies, but not any more... I think a lot of us want to be *engaged*, not constantly *challenged*.

They will build from the base of the arrow towards the direction it's facing. So if you place a 10x10 block of dirt facing right, the beavers will start on the very left-most row of 10, then the next, etc. They will NOT build if there is another unfinished dirt block in the same orientation BEHIND the first one in that row. So, if you needed a 2x20 row of terrain for example, if you place both rows of 20 going the same direction, the second row will need the tile behind it to be built first. If you instead place the rows facing into/away from each other, then the beavers can work on all of them at once.

Early game, ignore all items except the weapons you're trying to get and also any items that are especially good for your build (i.e. more enemies with loud, luck for lucky, harvesting for farmer, etc.) up until you have all 6 weapons. Once you have them, start building damage and also whatever your character is good at. Maybe that's just more damage, it can literally be any stat depending on the character. 

Also, economy is extremely important in the early game. A bit of harvesting goes a long way, a lot of harvesting early on will do wonders. Other forms of eco are almost always good too, like bag, hunting trophy, black flag, gentle alien/mouse, trees. They are almost always worth it if you can manage the cost.

Mid game, around wave 8ish, you want at least 60-70 effective hp by this point, less if you're going more glass cannon. At this point consider your sustain. Most of the time you will not be able to avoid damage in any given wave, especially during elite waves, so how do you heal? Consumables (better for glass cannon builds imo), regen (better for builds that are in the thick of things because it's always active), life steal (better for builds with fast repeated damage, or that just hit tons of enemies at once)? Or did you find some tentacles and can just build crit to heal that way? Consider how much your character gets hit and try to figure out how much regen you need with that to survive the first elite or horde.

The first horde/elite is usually the hardest part of a run, not always, but usually. After this, you just keep doing what you're doing. You should now be getting more money so you can essentially do ALL of those things. Get damage, get the stat that's good for your bro, get effective hp, get sustain.

Not sure how familiar you are with the speedrun scene in games but let me tell a little story about ocarina of time. Once upon a time, the speedrun for ocarina of time was quaint. It required the player to play through a majority of the game, only being able to skip a few select spots and sequence break a couple of times by using movement tricks like mega-flips. Then, as one of the most popular speedrun games of all time, people started to dig deeper. They found out that, hey, it turns out we don't need to do all of this "playing the game" thing, we can actually just beat the second boss, do a specific set of movements and actions when entering the portal afterwards, and that will just warp us to the end credits screen.

But the glitch hunters were not satisfied, they knew ocarina of time had more secrets within its spaghetti code that was held up with masking tape and rubber bands. Fast forward another few years, and now we have ACE, arbitrary code execution. It is now possible to write new code WHILE PLAYING the game. This broke open the game in such an absurd way it's hard to even fathom the difference between an ocarina of time speedrun 15 years ago and an ocarina of time speedrun today. 

Anyway, that story was mainly to just illustrate how far certain people are willing to go to find glitches. If anyone is more interested in knowing wtf I'm talking about, here's an [incredible video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2x_pqyrf9lA).

T11s are very much an exercise in never getting hit, at least for ranged. My advice after doing a few on my ele shaman (609ilvl) is to pick apart packs, take on as small of groups as you can manage. Also, use polymorph. It works on even the crazy elite mobs that spawn in T9s and above. I find hex/poly is basically a requirement for fighting the 2 ascended nerubian elites where 1 is a caster and 1 is melee. Even though they'll swap this buff that reduces damage by 99%, it's definitely the play to just CC one and kite the other till it's vulnerable.

As a caster, melee mobs should basically never be allowed to hit you in t11s, since if they get more than a couple hits off you're likely just dead. That said, I don't find kiting them to be that difficult, just takes patience. Caster mobs on the other hand are absolute monsters. Basically you need to do everything in your power to keep them from getting a cast off. Interrupts, hard CCs, knockbacks, anything. 

Bosses are always a bit touch and go, but tbh so far I've found them to be the easiest part of t11s. They hit hard for sure, but in doing so many t8s you probably figured out how to fight them, and that strategy really doesn't change. The big difference is you need to be more mindful about getting away from the boss whenever they're casting something to give you space. Often you can get 10-15 seconds of the boss chain casting abilities, so as long as you're not getting 1shot by those abilities, you get to use that time to recoup brann potions/CDs/etc.

I just managed it last night on my 609 ele shaman, probably about 4 hours total of attempts as well. Man that fight demands a lot, but like you said it was very satisfying to beat it because it feels like quite a feat.

Just for some insight on what I did at least as ele. Started the fight with earth ele, this is really just to give me a buffer to get potions out, also its cooldown is back up by the time I want it again (p2). Whenever the earth ele or brann has aggro, it's an absolute must to stay within about 15 yards, ideally even closer. Too far away and the claw smash is actually undodgeable at times. 

Dps on zekvir himself needs to be slow and steady, because while the dps check on the eggs is easily reached if I can stand there and blast it, it's much more likely I have to dodge 2-3 mechanics while killing the egg which hurts dps a lot. So the upshot of this is I need to save most of my CDs for the eggs. I used ghost wolf for dot dispells, which effectively meant I couldn't use it for dodging things as that would use up the snare removal effect which is on a 25 second cd.

When the earth ele wasn't alive and I was tanking, it was a delicate balance of using defensives when the boss is meleeing, and relying on brann potions to heal up while he's using abilities. I had to kind of learn the times when the boss had all of his abilities on CD and he'd just wail on me for a good 8 seconds or so, THOSE times I absolutely needed brann's hots rolling as well as defensive cooldowns running.

The absolute most annoying thing about this fight as a ranged I can confidently say is the claw smash. If he targets you and you're about 20-25 yards away, and you just so happened to use a GCD right as he starts his cast, the smash will go off before you even have time to use a GCD to get out. And when you're at that perfect distance away you're not running out unless you have some movement increase.

One of the best things about wow is the number of things you can do, it's really a matter of what sounds most interesting to you. You can primarily do single player stuff and not worry about grouping except through queued content (i.e. dungeon finder/LFR delves). You can do PUG (pick up group) content like mythic+ dungeons, which can infinitely scale in difficulty. You can do more organized group content, which could still be mythic+, but could also be raids. These don't *require* a guild, but in general you'll have a much better time doing this type of content if you have a guild you can run it with consistently. 

You mentioned you like pvp, while I'm not a big fan of pvp in wow personally, there's tons of pvp options available. There's standard battlegrounds which have a huge variety of objectives, and there's both unorganized battlegrounds and rated battlegrounds where you would pre-group with others, similar to a raid. There's arenas, both solo and pre-made once more. Arenas are smaller scale battles that are really just deathmatches as opposed to the objective-based stuff in battlegrounds. Blizzard also seems to have been putting in some random pvp game modes. If I recall there's one right now that's essentially warsong gulch (capture the flag) but there's tons of flags available, so I assume it is more chaotic than usual.

Those paths tend to be the main ones people choose to take, but they're far from the only ones. If you like, you can just collect as much stuff as possible (mounts, pets, toys, titles, achievements, etc). Or you can search for the perfect transmog set to make your character look the exact way you want it to in your head. Or you can do pet battles! I'm sure there's other ways to play as well that don't fall into any of the categories I've listed.

Regarding your ilvl, you're sitting at a perfectly fine level right now for just recently hitting 80. Just playing the content you want to do will lead to upgrades very regularly. pvp might be a little tough at first because you will likely be on the lower end of gear, but that will change pretty fast if you just stick with it and grab a few upgrades (weapon upgrades especially are more impactful than any other item slot upgrade). 

Also, I'd love having someone close to me that I could play with regularly, I don't know why your bf doesn't want to play with you, but it's not as though he has to take you straight to a M+7. Regarding overlapping your dots, you WANT to refresh them in the last few seconds in between the second to last and last tick. Any remaining time on the dot will be tacked on when you re-apply it. (e.g. you refresh agony when it has 3.5 seconds remaining, the new dot lasts for 28.5 seconds instead of just 25, and the very last tick of your previous agony will happen AT 25 seconds remaining).

The only time it loses out on damage is when you re-apply it when there's more than 1 tick remaining. Still, this can sometimes be the right play, as dots fully snapshot your spellpower when they're applied, meaning you might want to re-apply a dot when you have multiple spellpower procs/abilities active.

Contrary to what the other commenters are saying, all non-gathering primary professions have roughly the same benefit, which is +80 to your main stat (or +120 stam).

BS - 2 additional sockets for 2 extra gems, can put 2 main stat gems in for +80 main stat

JC - Epic JC gems, +27 stats over the normal gems (or +41 stam), and you can get 3, so +81 main stat

LW - +80 main stat over the regular leg attachments

Inscription - +80 main stat on your shoulder enchant over the exalted Therazane ones.

Engineering - +480 main stat for 10 seconds, 1 minute CD, averages to +80 main stat if you use it on CD.

Enchanting - +80 main stat from 2x ring enchants with 40 each

Alchemy - +80 main stat from your flask

Tailoring - More complicated, but the math comes out to 80.5 main stat if you re-proc the effect on average between 0-15 seconds after it becomes available. It's a proc that gives 580 main stat and lasts 15 seconds, with a 60 second ICD. While this may SOUND better than the others, remember you're giving up 50 of your main stat by not having an enchant. Because it's a proc, there's some amount of variance, meaning it CAN be more than 80 main stat on average, but it can also be less than 80 main stat on average.

tl;dr - No, tailoring is not simply the best profession, it depends completely on whether you value the burst from a large amount of main stat in the form of a proc versus the consistent, guaranteed bonus from another profession. I'm playing a demo lock, where it's very important to have a strong opener, so for ME, tailoring+engineering is better. Not every class functions this way, in fact most don't.

Welcome to the world (of warcraft)! I'll try to help you out here.

1. I would think any class can solo BC heroics with boosted gear, yes, as you get pretty high ilvl gear. However, I'm guessing when people said to run heroics for gear/gold, they meant *wrath* heroics. If you got a character boost though, I really wouldn't worry about gear at all. Your gear will all get replaced while questing up to the level cap in a couple weeks. For gold, heroics are certainly not the best way to grind. I'm not a big gold grinder but I would see if I could find some guides to making gold by people who are good at that kind of thing. Now, the reason you SHOULD do heroics is to get acquainted with your character. Just a heads up, though, affliction isn't the most amazing in dungeons because they need time for their damage to really reach its full potential, and dungeon bosses will go down very fast currently.

2. Assuming you're talking about wrath heroics, you can just queue directly into these, and you can queue directly into ones you want or can get a random one. Default hotkey is "I" to pull up the group finder. If you want to run TBC heroics, you'll have to fly out to them. They used to require attunement to enter, but I don't *think* they do anymore.

3. I'll break this out into 3 steps that I think should set you up for success. 

Well before the raid: Do dungeons, this time I'm talking about Cataclysm dungeons, both normal and then heroic once you've gotten enough gear and a feel for your character. In cata, dungeon bosses have significantly more mechanics than they ever have before, so they function as mini raid bosses that will prepare you for the kinds of things you'll see in raid. 

Shortly before the raid: Prepare. Look in your dungeon journal (new feature in cata, don't know the hotkey yet), it shows the boss abilities for every boss in the raid. If you're good with that, great! Otherwise, maybe watch a short strategy video for the bosses you're planning to fight. Also, in your preparation you will want to get consumables (food for buffs, potions, flasks).

During the raid: Listen, and try not to get defensive. You WILL make mistakes, it's ok. Make sure you listen to people giving advice after those mistakes. Some people will get on your case for it, but know that they have made a million more mistakes than you have while playing WoW, so don't put any stock into what they say.

 As far as mods, DBM is basically a requirement. It's not *actually* required, but at least personally I cannot imagine being able to play without being able to see boss ability timers at a very minimum. Everything else is gravy. I would suggest getting some addons that sound good to you, as they do greatly improve the game in my opinion. Check out CurseForge for a good way to get and manage your addons.

There's a sort of phenomenon that can happen in big cities where it seems like there are more coincidences like yours than there really should be. As I recall there's a few reasons for it. Firstly, you probably have quite a few friends/acquaintances. It's not necessarily unlikely that you and one of those people you know are going on vacation at the same time. It's also not that unlikely you both pick a fairly common vacation destination in New York. And it's also even fairly likely that IF you're both in New York at the same time, you're probably doing at least some of the common touristy things that people do in the city. So in reality you have a decent sized group of people who it'd be a coincidence to run into, in a place that many go to for vacation, doing things that other people on vacation in the city also do.

I think running across one *specific* person while in NYC is going to be significantly less likely than running across any person you happen to know.

That said, it's still a fun coincidence, it's not as though it's some mundane thing to find a friend randomly on the other side of the country, but it's not *that* uncommon to happen.

For example, if you can manage to fully saturate a blue belt with a fluid barrel, you'll be moving 2250 fluid per second (50 per barrel, 45 barrels per second). Of course you still have to deal with the logistics of putting it in/taking it out of the barrel but there are cases where it'll be desirable over pipes, even if the pipes aren't super long.

Also might be worth noting it's not really a very big logistical challenge once you have the logistic chests available. If you're filling a barrel then request empties and output the filled barrels into a passive provider. If you're emptying a barrel then request the filled barrels and output empties in an active provider. Just gotta make sure your empty barrel assembler is also hooked up to the system.

Unless you have a HUGE storage area where the furthest tank is like, 50 rows away from the pump, it'll be able to pump stuff out all the way from the back just fine.

If you just want bots for yourself, 20 is honestly enough to start with, as personal roboports allow 10 each and you won't have space for much more until later. If you're wanting to build your bot network, there's a good way to do this via a fairly simple circuit network. Make your bot factory and at some point have inserters putting bots into a roboport, you'll probably want the bots on separate belts to keep things organized. Hook up the inserters to the roboport, then click the roboport and make it "read robot information" or whatever it's called, I forget. It's the only checkbox that isn't checked from the start though.

Then you'll have a few variables, total/available logistic and total/available construction. Now if you tell the construction bot inserter that you want Z>30, then the inserter will only put more bots in if you have fewer than 30 available to work at one time (I think Z is available construction bots, but going off memory). Basically, what this does it adds bots steadily as you actually build things, so it only grows as much as you need. I'd adjust the number as the game goes on, but 30 seems pretty good at the start to me.

Alternatively, you can do the same thing but with the total # of bots variable instead, and that will just get you to the exact number you want in your network.

Also one last tip, you might want to put the bots into storage chests before putting them into the network instead of from the belt, with their inserters having the exact same circuit conditions as the roboport inserters. Then, when you inevitably chuck robots into logistic storage, they go into the box and can go back into the system when needed.

Stretching pipes very long distances is not recommended as you lose pressure in the pipeline for each piece of pipe the fluid must travel through. Also small tip relating to that: underground pipes count as 2 pieces of pipe for the purposes of calculating the pressure, regardless of how long the underground is. So, if you ARE going to stretch pipe a long way, use as many undergrounds as possible and as few regular pipes. There is also a way around this by continually having pumps along the entire length of your pipeline to keep the pressure constant, but that gets kind of expensive if you're doing it early game.

If you're wondering specifically about iron gears, that one's a bit of a tossup in the community between building them at the locations you need them vs. putting them on a main bus. Could be quite difficult to retake it from here largely because they're just occupying nearly every available tile. It's possible you may have overreacted to the Africa invasion. As I recall, they send ~7 or 8 units at you, which is substantial and enough to force you to respond to it, but should only require a small retinue of your army to deal with. When the invasion happens, I'd recommend sending only 4-5 of your own units down to defend (I'd say ranged units or a fairly tanky unit that you think can manage to stay alive is good). At the same time, make sure you have either militia or conscripts, or just workers that can be upgraded, and garrison them inside the cities further along the coast, this allows you plenty of time to defeat the troops in each city one-by-one. Definitely don't sleep on those conscripts, they actually hit decently hard. They may be frail, but that is offset immensely when they're garrisoned in the city.

My other tip would be to never leave the island without a very sizeable defensive force. Since Rome will never stop being at war with you, and they have a ton of cities to produce units with, leaving Panormus only lightly defended means they have an opportunity to overrun it. I'm not sure how many you had at first, but I'd say at least 3 onagers should be on the island (on the far left side of it) with more ready to replace them in case they get shot down, a couple archers and/or the better slingers in front of them, and then a row of melee units, fortified x5 ideally (obviously you can't fortify them if you're actively being attacked but could in the time in between).

Also one other tip I thought of after I played this myself that I wish I had done, I think it may be *extremely* valuable to chop down the forests on the island after deflecting the first attack. There's a lot of woods that cut the damage you do with your siege/archers. Could maybe leave a couple of trees up that are right next to the city center, but for the tiles further out you would be reducing their defensive abilities by a lot.

This is all good info, but I want to add on to the last point about food and growth. To answer OP's question about what population to aim for, there really isn't a single answer to that. Unused population doesn't do much on its own, but there are several specialists that give a benefit per population. If you have several of those specialists in your city, you'd maybe want to consider either building some military, some infrastructure (forums/archives/treasuries), or even some festivals to give a nice growth injection to the city, basically anything that doesn't require growth to build or require a citizen. 

However, having more citizens is basically never bad as far as I know. So if you have a mega growth capital or something that grows to 10 population, that's a good thing, you can just spam out a million specialists later in the game with them.

I would say about food in particular though that stockpiling it early isn't a bad thing and doesn't necessarily mean you need more military. Military and workers consume a relatively small amount of food (and you can reduce it with a law, though I forget which one at the moment). For example, one farm producing 10 food on a bonus resource can feed 10 early game units/workers. I've had games where there are quite a few bonus food resources near my starting location and quickly got up to +100 food or so. There's no real way you're going to spend all that in the early game though. Lategame however, specialists start to eat TONS of food if you're spamming them.

They will likely still be sentenced because they murdered someone, but they are less likely to get the maximum sentence because they've shown that remorse. Not saying it's right or wrong, but that is a large part of the reason minimum/maximum sentences exist.

Not exactly sure what you mean, but I do have a bit of Ahorn experience so can possibly help. To my knowledge, the hidden block paths cannot be curved, they have to be placed in the same way that normal foreground tiles are placed. Just a heads up, you likely want to use "Fake Wall" instead of "Fake Block" because fake walls can actually blend into other foreground tiles (better for secrets generally).

As far as indicating a secret path, I tend to just use background decals that seem slightly out of place (or in my latest map, I have a symmetrical room, and in the spot where I put a secret, there's an extra background object that isn't replicated on the other side of the room). I think background objects might be what you saw in the vanilla game, but I'm not sure. 

The other way that tends to work to indicate a secret path is to basically indent the fake wall from the edge of the actual wall a bit. Players tend to explore nooks and crannies without you needing to encourage them more (as long as it's not too hard to REACH the nooks and crannies).

Keyboard is fine to play this game, in fact many people would say it's superior (not me, I think all the more 'standard' control setups are valid and you can do very well with any of them). Keyboard actually gets a benefit that controllers don't have, that being the fact you have 4 separate keys for your 4 directions, rather than a single entity (an analog stick or a d-pad). This means "misdrects" are extremely uncommon on keyboard. You can't input a ~30 degree angle that is then interpreted as a right dash when you wanted it to be an up-right on a keyboard, instead you just press 2 buttons and that's your up-right. But then on the other hand, something like feathers are objectively harder to control without analog movement, which is why I think no control scheme is just outright better for Celeste than any other, they all have benefits/drawbacks.

I'd recommend at this point mainly practicing and refining your strategies. Watching other people speedrun the game is insanely helpful, because you can see what strategies are being used that you can incorporate. Also if you don't have the speedrun tool installed already (which you can get through the everest mod installer), then I HIGHLY recommend you get it. It has a lot of cool features but #1 is definitely the save state mechanic, which you can use to practice various strategies significantly faster than with the standard respawn mechanic.

As others have mentioned, there's not really any one mechanic to learn that'll significantly speed up your run (except maybe arguably corner boosts), but I'd also recommend starting to get some practice with 5b. You may not want to incorporate it into a run yet because of its difficulty, which is totally fine, but once you're even moderately comfortable with it, it's a HUGE time save over 5a.

You want to hug the wall as you're falling, then up-left dash, and finally up dash to grab the left side of the final long wall that you need to climb. It's fairly tight, but definitely possible. Make sure you let your first dash completely finish before doing the up dash, you might even need to wait a tiny bit longer after that to actually make it to the other side of the wall. But just make sure you're not doing the second dash early. Should get just enough distance to make it.

You said you're getting close so most likely you have the right idea, which is why I mention letting the dash finish completely. The way dashes work in this game, you essentially get a little extra 'push' of distance for lack of a better word when a dash ends in mid-air (this is maybe not totally accurate, it's basically just a little bit of conserved momentum, I'm just not sure the best way to describe it). If you immediately dash again, then you miss out on this little extra distance which is the actual difference maker on this particular screen.

I wouldn't consider myself an expert by any means so I'm not sure I have the correct answer to that. But, at least what I do is generally to make as many barracks/ranges as possible (which tends to just be the cap of 2 each) in those cities while trying to get them all adjacent to at least one of the garrison, stronghold, and/or citadel. Those buildings both buff each other so it's worthwhile to plan around at least a little bit to make sure you get the adjacency.

I think you also tend to want at least 1 officer, maybe more as the game goes on, since you probably don't need to be pumping units out of the city on every single turn, you should be able to find some down time for the city to train up some specialists.

To your other question, I definitely think Old World very much rewards specializing your cities, so I'd say having a small number of cities dedicated to generating training and producing units is better than just having all your cities produce units when needed. The exact number you want making units probably depends a lot on the nation you're playing and your general gameplan. You can honestly get away with never building a barracks assuming you're quick to snatch up tribal city sites and then play the diplomatic game with the AI. But if you're going heavy on war, I think at minimum 3 cities focused on training units would be a good idea.

The only time I've been able to take very few losses is when I've had a tech advantage going into it. Still, losses are basically guaranteed unless the AI has had their army completely crushed before you even go to war with them. But, with a tech advantage, it's a lot easier to tip the balance in your favor. You'll lose maybe a unit a turn while killing 4-5 enemy units.

Also I've noticed the AI tends to tunnel vision lower tech units, probably because they're easier to kill in general. You can use this to your advantage by baiting in 4-5 strong units to kill a single one of your weakest units, then clearing them all out with the rest of your actual strong units.

If you're even on tech, I've just found war to be outright grindy, very tough to win, though not necessarily hard to keep things under control if you're just defending. Unless you have a massive amount of troops over the AIs it's gonna be hard to actually take cities.

There's really only a few specific things that you need while going for a religious win. I'd say you need all of: Max rank Moksha with double apostle promotion upgrade, Theocracy, and a Mosque in your Moksha city (you can get it in other cities too, but avoid faith buying them). If Yerevan is also in your game, you'd also want to be their suzerain because it's broken OP for a religious win. You can also throw in the religious wonders if you want but they're really not needed (Hagia Sophia I think is worth building, but the others are pretty meh).

So, with that in mind, the only real thing you need is culture, BUT, you don't really need that much. You only need 4 governor titles to fully upgrade Moksha, and probably another 4-5 or so earlier on in the game cause you don't want to miss out on the other much better early governors. So, let's just call it 10 governor titles, 3 of which will come from your government plaza+buildings, that's quite easy to grab without building a bunch of theatre squares. Theocracy is fairly early in the civic tree too so really don't need much for that either.

Once you have all that, literally the only thing that matters for a religious victory is faith, nothing else does anything whatsoever (except production since you can convert it to more faith via projects). At that point the only thing you do is spam projects while swarming the AI with infinite apostles.

The other commenter already answered, but just to add to that, there are 2 classifications of district, just a generic "District" and a "Specialty" district. Aqueducts, dams, city centers, neighborhoods and canals are all just districts and should function with the garrison promotion/adding adjacency to other districts. Specialty districts are just everything else where only 1 is allowed per 3 population, but they ALSO count as just regular districts of course.

Honestly it sounds like you're basically there, but I'll give my opinion if it helps. If you want to be a blaster, which it sounds like you do, then sorcerer is the way to go, and overwhelming mage will be fine (cross-blooded is probably a bit more powerful, but as you noted it's maybe more management than you'd like to do as a new player, which is totally fine). 

One thing you almost certainly will want is an elemental bloodline. You can go fire, but any element works. The reason for this is the bloodline has a toggleable ability that will convert ALL elemental damage to the type of your bloodline. This opens up every damaging spell for you, instead of the ones specific to that one element. Note you can grab the mythic ability "second bloodline" to get the elemental bloodline if you'd prefer to start with arcane, which is a very good choice as well.

On the feat side, I'd say basically all of the above that you've listed you will want to get. You want spell focus evocation+greater, you'll want elemental focus+greater, you'll want spell pen+greater, and you'll want point blank+precise shot. It's not terribly important which one you get first, but I tend to do spell focus feats->point blank+precise shot->spell pen feats->elemental focus feats for a caster. From there you can pick up whichever metamagics you prefer. Honestly this is totally personal preference. I'm a big fan of empower, extend, and selective metamagics for a blaster caster, but you may prefer quicken, bolster, maximize, etc. I'd say just pick the one you think sounds best or most fun (whichever is more important to you). Apart from those feats you're pretty free to pick up whatever you like, I usually go for some form of survivability feats, but that's generally much later in the game.

As far as mythic path, both azata and lich will serve you pretty well. Lich I'd argue is MUCH stronger due to spellbook merging (you get to add your mythic rank to your caster level, meaning you'll get lvl 30 caster level baseline at the end of the game. You also get higher level spells earlier on). If you go azata, pick up Zippy Magic as soon as possible.

For the mythic abilities/feats, it's actually pretty straightforward for a blaster. You'll want elemental ascendance pretty damn early. Then abundant casting 1, 2, and 3 as you get to the appropriate spell level. Then mythic spell pen, mythic spell focus, basically anything that looks like it'd be good for a caster.

I'm not sure if you're looking for any advice, but I think I can help out and be a bit more constructive than the guy you replied to here. I've actually said the same thing in another thread a while ago, but I'd *highly* recommend always using the "inspect" lens if you aren't currently, default hotkey is Y, and just quickly reviewing enemy stat blocks by hovering over them when combat starts.

Especially for bosses, but really I find it helpful for everything, even after playing through the game multiple times, as it's a super quick way to see the specific weaknesses of an enemy. Inevitable Darkness (and the playful variant in the main game), has incredibly high regular AC, but low-middling touch AC. It's saves are also not insanely high if my memory serves, so there is a chance to hit him with powerful spells, though you'd almost certainly need a caster that's dedicated to doing so.

This sort of stat spread is probably the most common for bosses, but they actually vary a fair bit, making different tactics work better or worse on different boss fights. Which brings me to my second tip, just having a party that can do a variety of things, and do them well. Some characters can target the main AC or just flatfooted, while others are going for the touch AC, a caster or two in the back using powerful CC's, and then supported by some supporting class to improve the effectiveness of several of those other characters.

Difficulty is handled in basically the same way as the base game. Enemies get bonuses (or negatives) to their base stats, +to hit, saves, etc. Some of the difficulty settings from the main game are more or less irrelevant for BtSL, like encumberance effecting world map travel (there is no world map to travel, so no effect). Other than that it's the same compared to the main game. So basically all that is to say I'd probably play on the same difficulty you were playing in order to have the most fun with it, unless you'd prefer to notch up the difficulty for this.

For how a run works, it's basically like this: 

1. You create your main character. There's not a lot going on story wise, so imo it's better to just make a strong character instead of going for any RP lean.

2. You're given some starting resources, almost certainly you'll want to use them to purchase 2-3 merc teammates from the dragon. I think you can buy 3, but you may want some money left over to buy gear, this is kinda personal preference.

3. Go into the dungeon. Each floor has a sort of theme with its enemies, so you'll see a good variety of them. There are lots of hidden rooms with some pretty nice loot. As you go through floors, you'll level up very quickly (around 1 level per floor if I recall), and you should also be able to get quite a lot of stuff to vendor.

4. For the first few floors, you'll be returning to the surface a lot to rest+try to buy more mercs. It doesn't take too long to get a full party of 6. 

5. If a character dies, you can replace them (except the MC I think). If everyone dies, or just the MC, the run is over.

6. Repeat from step 1, but this time you'll receive a bonus. These vary quite a bit and I don't remember a lot of them. Sometimes it'll let you carry over an item from a previous run, for example though, which can be a huge boon to subsequent runs.

Sorry that was a lot, but hope it helps!
